worksheet.title: The Wrong Turn
worksheet.subtitle: Ontario Math C3.2 — read, find, and fix code
worksheet.learning_goal: I can fix a turtle shape loop with the wrong turn angle.

parts.title: Wrong turn, open shape
text: In a turtle shape, each shape needs the right turn: square 90, triangle 120, pentagon 72, hexagon 60.
If the turn is wrong, the shape will not close. Even when the range is right, the shape can still look wrong — so check the turn.

parts.title: This should draw a TRIANGLE — but it's buggy
parts.output: The corners are wrong — the triangle does not close.

parts.caption: right 90 won't make a triangle; right 120 closes it.

parts.title: Find the bug
parts.prompt: The triangle code uses right(90). A triangle needs right 120. What should right() be? ______

parts.title: Fix the hexagon
parts.prompt: This should draw a hexagon (6 sides):  for i in range(6): bit.forward(40); bit.right(90). A hexagon needs right 60. What is wrong, and what should the turn be?

parts.title: Write the fix
parts.prompt: Bit should draw a pentagon (5 sides). The turn for a pentagon is 72. Write it:  bit.right(______)

parts.title: Challenge
parts.prompt: A SQUARE loop has right(60) instead of right(90). Will the square close? Why not? What should the turn be?

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: Each shape has its own turn. If the shape does not close, the turn is probably wrong — match the turn to the shape (square 90, triangle 120, …).

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: Students debug shape loops where the TURN is wrong, so the shape will not close. The correct turns are given: square 90, triangle 120, pentagon 72, hexagon 60. The method here is SHOULD → DOES → FIX: say what the code SHOULD do, run it to see what it DOES, then FIX the one thing that is wrong. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start
parts.text: No computer needed — the worksheet shows the code and what Bit should do. Optional: a Scratch-style app (for the block loops) or a free Python-turtle playground (for the shapes) to run the code — you only press Run.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 30 minutes)
text: 1. Show it (you do). Each shape needs its own turn; the wrong turn leaves the shape open.
2. Do one together. Exercise 1 — a triangle needs turn right 120, not 90.
3. Let them work. Students fix a hexagon turn (Ex 2), a pentagon turn (Ex 3), and explain a square that will not close (Ex 4).

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercise 1 — turn right 120. Exercise 2 — the turn is wrong; change it to turn right 60.
Exercise 3 — turn right 72. Exercise 4 (challenge) — no, it will not close; turn right 60 is a hexagon turn — a square needs turn right 90.

parts.title: If students get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: changing the number of sides instead of the turn. Here the sides are right; the turn is wrong.
Make it easier: keep a small chart of the four shape turns nearby.
Make it harder: ask the turn for a shape not on the chart (e.g. eight sides → 45).

parts.title: Ontario curriculum link (official wording)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events.
In plain terms: students write and run step-by-step instructions — including a "repeat" instruction — to make something happen.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.
In plain terms: students read instructions, find what is wrong, fix it, and explain what the change did.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The child gives each shape its correct turn so it closes.
